Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: This item appears misclassified within the Threat node because it describes an avoidance behaviour rather than a threat appraisal or sense of current danger. Given the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, so threat items should plausibly drive coping responses; this item itself is already a maladaptive strategy and duplicates the behavioural content of the Maladaptive Strategies node. The other Threat items (flashbacks, scanning exits) reflect re-experiencing/current danger more coherently for torture trauma.

vignette:
Shanti was twenty-six years old when she was taken, though she had stopped counting the days by the time she was released. She had been a tailor in a small shop in her hometown, her hands steady with needle and thread, her days measured by the rhythm of fabrics and orders. The men who came for her were not strangers-they were known to the neighborhood, part of a local political faction that had been consolidating power through fear. They accused her of passing information to a rival group, a charge she had never fully understood. What she remembered most clearly was the room: windowless, concrete, with a single bulb that never went out. For three weeks, they questioned her, beat her, and kept her in a state of constant sensory deprivation broken only by pain. She learned to stop expecting night, stop expecting rescue, stop expecting anything at all. When she was finally let go-dumped on a roadside outside the city-she walked until she found a bus station, her body bruised but her mind already beginning to fracture in ways she would not recognize for months.

Her husband had arranged for her to come to the United States on a spousal visa soon after. He was a quiet man, a mechanic, and he had done his best to give her a new life. But Shanti could not feel safe. In their small apartment in a midwestern city, she found herself scanning every room before she could sit down. The first time she walked into a grocery store, her eyes darted to the emergency exits, counting them, measuring the distance, noting whether the doors pushed outward or inward. She had never done this before. Now she did it without thinking, every single time. She could not sit with her back to a door. She could not tolerate silence-the absence of sound felt like the concrete room-but she also could not tolerate noise that she could not control. Her husband's television in the next room, a casual comedy, would make her chest tighten until she had to leave.

She stopped going to the doctor. She had developed a persistent pain in her lower back, likely from the beatings, but the thought of a clinic-of being asked to undress, of a stranger's hands near her body-sent her into a cold sweat. She told her husband she was fine. She told herself the pain was nothing. She had come to believe that any situation where she was not in control of her own body was a trap, and she would rather live with the pain than walk into one. She also stopped leaving the house for anything other than necessities. Her husband brought home groceries. She sewed from their living room, taking in alterations for neighbors, working on a machine she had bought secondhand. It was the only thing that felt familiar, the only time her hands remembered what to do without her mind racing.

But even sewing became difficult when she felt a strong emotion. If a customer complained, or if her husband raised his voice in frustration about a broken car part, Shanti would feel her throat close. She would put the fabric down, walk to the bathroom, and sit on the floor until the feeling passed. She had learned that strong emotions-any strong emotion-were dangerous. They blurred her vision, made her heart pound, and brought back the smell of the concrete room. She could not afford to feel. So she avoided anything that might make her feel: arguments, surprises, even moments of tenderness that were too intense. Her husband began to pull away, confused and hurt. He did not understand why she flinched when he touched her shoulder, why she would not let him hold her for more than a few seconds.

Relaxation itself had become terrifying. The few times she had tried to rest-to lie down on the couch with her eyes closed, to let her mind drift-she had been yanked back into the room by a flashback so vivid she could feel the rope around her wrists. She learned to stay busy, to keep her hands moving, to never let her guard down. Being alert felt like survival. Letting go felt like death.

What finally brought her to a clinic was not her own decision. Her husband had found her one afternoon on the kitchen floor, shaking, her eyes open but unseeing, muttering in a language he barely understood. He had called a crisis line, and a caseworker had helped him find a therapist who worked with survivors of torture. Shanti came to the first session because she was too exhausted to refuse. She sat with her back to the wall, her eyes fixed on the door, and told the therapist that she was not sure she could be helped. What she did not say-what she could not yet say-was that she was terrified of what would happen if she stopped being afraid. She had built her survival around vigilance, and she did not know who she would be without it.
